title: The first jhana
hook: like bath powder kneaded with water until it is soaked through: joy filling the body (MN 39)

segments.voice: Yesterday: samadhi, and your line, gathered. Did you do one thing with your whole attention, and did anything change? Day three hundred ninety-six.

A boy sits in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father is busy with the work of the day. Nobody is watching him. And something happens: his mind goes quiet and bright, and his body fills with a gentle joy. Years later, after a long stretch of starving himself and pushing his body to its limit, that grown man remembers the afternoon under the tree, and wonders: could that be the way to awakening? Today: the first jhana.
screen: `UNDER THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` → `QUIET, BRIGHT, GLAD.` → `COULD THAT BE THE WAY?`

segments.voice: The man is the Buddha-to-be, and he tells this story himself, in MN 36. He'd been wary of that kind of pleasure, he says; then he saw he didn't need to fear it, because it had nothing to do with sense pleasures. Jhana is the Pali word. In Sanskrit it's dhyana, the same word that traveled to China as chan and to Japan as zen. It means meditative absorption. In MN 39 the Buddha describes the first one: quite secluded from sense pleasures and unwholesome states, a person enters the first jhana, with directed and sustained thought, and with joy and pleasure born of that seclusion. Then he gives a picture from a world before bars of soap. A skilled bath attendant pours bath powder into a metal bowl, sprinkles it with water, bit by bit, and kneads it into a ball, until the moisture soaks every grain, inside and out, yet doesn't drip. That's how this joy fills the body. Look at the picture closely. The joy is physical: the text says it drenches and fills the whole body. It's thorough: no part is left dry. It's contained: nothing leaks. And there's still a hand at work. Thinking is still present in the first jhana, directed and sustained, like the attendant's hands working the powder. The later jhanas let even that settle. One honest note: teachers today disagree about how deep this state is. Some describe a rare, total absorption; others a calmer, more accessible steadiness. The texts give pictures, not a depth gauge.
screen: `JHANA, DHYANA, CHAN, ZEN.` · `SECLUDED, YET STILL THINKING.` · `BATH POWDER SOAKED THROUGH.` · `TEACHERS DIFFER ON HOW DEEP.` · then, large: `SOAKED THROUGH.`

segments.voice: No need to reach for joy. Just look for any ease in the body that's already here. Maybe the hands are warm. Maybe the shoulders let go a little on the out-breath. Maybe the belly is soft. Find one small place of ease, and see whether it can spread, slowly, like water into powder, one grain at a time. If you find nothing, that's honest too: rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Jhana. Meditative absorption. In the first, joy born of seclusion soaks the whole body, like water kneaded into bath powder.
Your line: soaked through. Once today, when something feels good, a warm cup, sun on your face, let it soak in for three breaths before you move on. Day three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Jhana practice is taught especially in Theravada meditation lineages, usually with a teacher and often on retreat; Chan and Zen take their names from the same word, dhyana.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the first jhana.

myth: jhana and zen come from the same word
Pali jhana, Sanskrit dhyana, Chinese chan, Japanese zen.
in the first jhana all thinking has stopped
directed and sustained thought are still present; they settle later.
the Buddha remembered something like the first jhana from his childhood
MN 36: under a rose-apple tree, while his father was busy.

fork.setup: after years of harsh practice, you remember a quiet joy from your childhood. what does the Buddha-to-be decide, in MN 36?
options: that pleasure is dangerous and must be avoided
that this might be the way, and he needn't fear it
that he should go home to his father
fork.reveal: he saw that this joy had nothing to do with sense pleasures, so there was no need to fear it, and he took it as a path.

original.note: Pali jhāna: meditative absorption; Sanskrit dhyāna (ध्यान), which became Chinese chan and Japanese zen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trance where the world disappears.
what it means: a gathered absorption that, in the first jhana, still has thought, and soaks the body with joy.

what a scholar hears: the first jhāna's qualities are listed as vitakka and vicāra, directed and sustained thought, with pīti and sukha, joy and pleasure, born of seclusion; MN 43 adds one-pointedness.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the bath powder simile)
Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the memory under the rose-apple tree)
Majjhima Nikaya 43, Mahavedalla Sutta (the factors of the first jhana)

notes: MN 36 says the boyhood memory came while his father 'the Sakyan was occupied'; the commentary places it at a plowing festival. The script says only 'busy with the work of the day'.
'Six years' of austerities is the traditional figure; please confirm wording.
MN 43 listing one-pointedness among first-jhana factors: please confirm.
Modern disagreement about jhana depth is stated generally, without naming teachers.
